metaDescription: Six SD cards for cameras compared on speed class, UHS-I versus UHS-II, write speed and capacity, with notes on what 4K video and burst shooting really need.
expertTake: The SanDisk Extreme PRO 128GB is our top pick because its V30 and U3 labels cover 4K video and burst photography on most cameras, with a capacity that lasts a day of shooting. The SanDisk Ultra 64GB is the value pick for point-and-shoot cameras and Full HD video. Skip UHS-II cards unless your camera has the second row of pins, because in a UHS-I camera they simply run at UHS-I speed.
introParagraphs: An SD card is the part of a camera system that fails quietly: a card that is too slow drops frames in video or stalls during a burst, and a card that fails can lose a shoot. The right card matches your camera's speed support and your recording format.

This guide compares SD cards on speed class, UHS bus, write speed and capacity. We explain why advertised read speed is not the number that matters for recording, and how to choose a card that fits your camera instead of paying for speed it cannot use.

products.name: SanDisk 128GB Extreme PRO SD Card UHS-I V30 U3 Up to 250MB/s Read
products.description:
The Extreme PRO 128 GB is a UHS-I card with V30 and U3 labels and a stated read speed of up to 250 MB/s. The V30 rating means a minimum sustained write of 30 MB/s, which is the number that matters for 4K video. It comes in capacities up to 2 TB, and 128 GB is a sensible all-day size for most shooters.

The tradeoff is that the headline read speed describes offloading to a computer, not recording, and it only reaches that speed with a fast reader and a compatible host. A UHS-I bus caps below UHS-II cards such as the Lexar Silver PRO. It costs more than the SanDisk Ultra line. It suits photographers and videographers who shoot 4K or bursts and want a reliable mainstream card.

Format the card in the camera, not on a computer, so the file structure matches. Copy files off after each shoot and avoid deleting on the camera. Replace a card that shows errors rather than trusting it for a client job.

products.name: SanDisk 64GB Ultra SD Card UHS-I U1 Up to 145MB/s Read for Full HD
products.description:
The SanDisk Ultra 64 GB is aimed at compact and mid-range cameras, with U1 and Class 10 labels and Full HD video. U1 guarantees a minimum sustained write of 10 MB/s, which suits 1080p recording and normal photography. The maker states read speeds up to 145 MB/s, a figure that matters for offloading.

The tradeoff is headroom. U1 is not enough for 4K video or fast bursts on many cameras, and a 64 GB card fills sooner with high-resolution files. Compared with the Extreme PRO, it saves money but limits sustained write. It suits point-and-shoot cameras, family photos and Full HD clips.

Check your camera's manual for the speed class it needs. Keep a second card as a spare. Format in the camera and copy files off regularly.

products.name: SanDisk 128GB Ultra SDXC UHS-I Memory Card 100MB/s C10 U1
products.description:
The 128 GB Ultra SDXC is a straightforward UHS-I card with Class 10 and U1 labels and a stated read speed of 100 MB/s. It is aimed at compact to mid-range cameras and Full HD video, and the maker notes that Full HD support depends on the host device. The 128 GB size doubles the 64 GB option.

The tradeoff is again sustained write. U1 is the floor for Full HD, and it will not support 4K recording on cameras that require U3. Compared with the 64 GB Ultra, it carries twice the capacity at a higher price. It suits travelers who want more storage without a performance upgrade.

Format in the camera. Keep a second card for backup. Replace the card if it throws errors.

products.name: SanDisk 64GB Extreme PRO SDXC UHS-I C10 U3 V30 4K UHD
products.description:
The Extreme PRO 64 GB brings V30 and U3 labels to a smaller capacity, with a stated read speed of up to 200 MB/s and write speed of up to 90 MB/s. The write figure is lower than the larger 256 GB model, which is typical for smaller flash cards. It offers the 4K-ready rating at a lower price than the larger cards.

The tradeoff is capacity. 64 GB holds less 4K video, so you may need to swap cards midday. Compared with the 128 GB Extreme PRO, it saves money but fills quickly. It suits casual 4K shooters and photographers who do not shoot long clips.

Pair it with a UHS-I reader for the stated speeds. Format in camera and offload after each shoot. Carry a second card.

products.name: SanDisk 256GB Extreme PRO SD Card UHS-I V30 U3 Up to 140MB/s Write
products.description:
The 256 GB Extreme PRO states a read speed of up to 200 MB/s and a write speed of up to 140 MB/s, the highest write figure among the UHS-I cards here. The V30 and U3 labels cover 4K video and bursts, and the 256 GB capacity suits a full day or multiple shoots between offloads. It works with the maker's QuickFlow offload technology when paired with a recommended reader.

The tradeoff is risk and price. A large card means more footage on one card, so a failure loses more, and it is the most expensive here. Compared with the 128 GB Extreme PRO, it offers faster stated write and double the capacity. It suits wedding, event and travel shooters who need to avoid card swaps.

Copy files off often and do not fill the card to the last gigabyte. Keep a second card for backup. Format in camera.

products.description:
The Lexar Silver PRO is a UHS-II card with V60 and U3 labels and stated speeds of up to 280 MB/s read and 120 MB/s write. UHS-II cards use a second row of pins, which lets them run much faster in cameras that support it. The V60 rating means a minimum sustained write of 60 MB/s, suitable for higher bitrate 4K video.

The tradeoff is compatibility and price. In a UHS-I camera the card runs at UHS-I speed, so the extra cost is wasted unless your camera supports UHS-II. Compared with the Extreme PRO, it targets high bitrate video and fast bursts. It suits owners of UHS-II mirrorless cameras who need V60 writes.

Check your camera's manual for UHS-II support before buying. Use a UHS-II reader for full offload speed. Format in camera and keep a spare.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Speed classes tell you the minimum sustained write: U1 is 10 MB/s, U3 is 30 MB/s, V30 is 30 MB/s and V60 is 60 MB/s. The SanDisk Ultra is U1 and the Extreme PRO and Lexar are U3 and above. For 4K video, look for U3 or V30. Check your camera manual for a line about the speed class or bus it supports, because that line decides everything else. If it says UHS-I only, a UHS-II card is a waste of money and a V30 card is already the practical ceiling.

UHS-II cards use a second row of pins and run faster in cameras that support it. The Lexar Silver PRO is UHS-II, while the SanDisk cards are UHS-I. In a UHS-I camera a UHS-II card drops to UHS-I speed. Record a short test clip at your highest quality setting before an important shoot, then check it plays back cleanly. A card that drops frames during a test will drop them during the event too.

The headline 250 MB/s or 280 MB/s is read speed for offloading to a computer. Recording depends on write speed and the speed class. A fast read number does not make a card record faster. Do not read the speed number on the label as a promise for your camera, because cameras write at their own pace and the card only has to be fast enough. A faster card does not make a slow camera quicker.

64 GB suits casual shooters, 128 GB suits a day of shooting, and 256 GB suits long events. Larger cards risk more footage on one card. Choose a size you are comfortable losing. Capacity should reflect how you offload. If you copy files to a laptop every night, a 64 GB card goes a long way, while if you travel without a laptop, a larger card or several cards helps.

SDHC cards go up to 32 GB and SDXC cards are above 32 GB, using exFAT. Check that your camera supports SDXC and the speed class it needs. Older cameras may reject large cards. Camera-specific notes matter, since some bodies need a V60 card for their highest bitrate or all-intra video modes. The camera manual or maker's support page names the card requirement.

Format the card in the camera, copy files off often and avoid deleting on the camera. Cards fail suddenly, so keep a spare. Replace cards that throw errors. Keep your cards in their cases, write on them with a permanent marker and rotate them, so a single card does not carry all the wear.

howWeEvaluated.title: Specification review
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared published speed classes, bus types, read and write speeds and capacities. We read each listing for host requirements. We set the SanDisk Extreme PRO against the Lexar Silver PRO. We also read how each maker describes write speed versus read speed.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at recurring themes in owner feedback such as slow writes, counterfeit cards and compatibility. Single complaints were set aside. We did not use star ratings. We also checked which cards state a V rating, since it signals video support.

howWeEvaluated.title: Design approach
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered how each card fits camera needs, from Full HD to 4K and UHS-II. We also looked at capacity choices. We also kept camera compatibility in mind when ranking options.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and price position
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the cards by relative price tier and asked what each step up adds. We did not quote prices. We also compared how each card handles capacity trade-offs.

howWeEvaluated.title: What we did not do
howWeEvaluated.description: We did not record video or run speed benchmarks on these cards. Scores are editorial judgments built on published information. Speed figures remain makers' claims. We also noted where listings use internal testing language.

maintenance.why: A camera-made file structure avoids errors. Formatting on a computer can cause issues. Label each card with a number so you can track which one has errors.
Cards can fail suddenly. A second copy is the real backup. A soft cloth keeps the gold contacts clean.
Dust and static damage contacts. A case protects them. Do not leave cards in a hot car or in direct sun.
A card that throws errors is a warning. Replace it. Eject safely from the computer before pulling the card.
Counterfeit cards report false capacity. Authorized sellers reduce this risk. Order replacements from the maker or an authorized store.

faq.q: Do I need a UHS-II card?
faq.a: Only if your camera supports UHS-II. Otherwise it runs at UHS-I speed. If a card ever shows an error message, copy what you can off it right away and retire it, because cards often fail further once they start giving trouble.

Video Speed Class 30, a minimum sustained write of 30 MB/s, suited to 4K video. Most cameras stop recording or show a slow card warning when the card cannot keep up, so watch for that warning rather than guessing.

faq.q: How much capacity do I need?
faq.a: 64 GB for casual shooting, 128 GB for a day of 4K or stills and 256 GB for long events. A card reader is not a luxury if you offload often, since built-in laptop readers are often slower than a proper USB 3 reader.

faq.q: Is a faster read speed better for recording?
faq.a: No. Recording depends on write speed and speed class. Read speed affects offloading. Cards can be written to many thousands of times, but wear is real, and heavy shooters replace cards every few years as a precaution.

faq.q: Can I use a microSD card in a camera?
faq.a: Only with an adapter, and many cameras need full-size SD cards. Check the camera slot. Use cards from the same maker in a pair if your camera has two slots, which keeps behavior predictable in a backup mode.

faq.q: How do I avoid counterfeit cards?
faq.a: Buy from the maker or an authorized seller, and test capacity with a checker tool before filing important work. When you travel, pack spare cards in a separate bag from the camera, so a lost bag does not take everything.
